Integers go to PARI. One `factor` works for integers, rationals and
polynomials, and the arithmetic functions have their textbook names.

## Factorisation

```{er2}
f = factor(2^64 + 1)
print(f)
print(list(f), f.value() == 2^64 + 1)
```

Negative numbers and rationals factor too:

```{er2}
print(factor(-360), factor(3/20))
```

A factorisation is a mathematical object, so it displays as one:

```{er2}
factor(720)
```

A partial factorisation stops trial division at a limit, and says what it
could not split:

```{er2}
g = factor(10^60 + 1, limit=10^5)
print(g)
print(g.is_complete, g.unfactored)
```

## Arithmetic functions

```{er2}
n = 360
print(divisors(n)[:6], numdiv(n), sigma(n), phi(n), radical(n))
```

## Primes

$2^{127} - 1$ is prime, and so is $2^{521} - 1$, the first Mersenne prime
found by computer:

```{er2}
isprime(2^127 - 1), isprime(2^521 - 1)
```

The primes below 50, in ordinary Python:

```{er2}
[k for k in range(50) if isprime(k)]
```

## In prose

$\varphi(123456789) =$ `{er2} phi(123456789)`, and
$360 =$ `{er2} latex(factor(360))`.
